subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage:
“Kishore, where's Papa?” asked Ujjwal, walking across the room. Kishore's eyes followed him step by step.
“Look, Kishore. Kite!” Ujjwal pointed out of the window at a red kite over the rooftops.
Kishore turned his head to the window, then back at his father's face. “Kite,” he said, pointing too.
“Yes, kite! You saw it.”
Kishore kept watching until the red shape slid behind the water tank.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal point at through the window?
qa.a: A red kite over the rooftops.

qa.q: What does Kishore's glance back at his father seem to show?
qa.a: It seems to show he was interested and wanted to share the sight with Ujjwal. It could also be that he was checking whether the word Ujjwal used was the right one.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do next to keep the shared looking going?
qa.a: He could point at other things, say their names, and pause to see whether Kishore looks where he points.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel when Kishore follows his point?
qa.a: He is likely to feel delighted and connected, because his son is looking with him and not just at him. 🙂

grounding: A toddler tracks a parent with his eyes and follows a point to share attention on an object.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage: Playgroup note, Friday. Ayesha, almost two, watched me across the room while I set out cups, turning her head as I moved. When I pointed to the picture of a cat on the wall and said “Look, a cat,” she looked at the cat, then at me, and pointed too. She stayed with the picture for a long moment. I said “cat” again and waved at it. I will tell her mother how well she looks along with us. 🙂 Kavitha

qa.q: Who wrote the note, and what did Ayesha look at after the pointing?
qa.a: Kavitha wrote it, and Ayesha looked at the picture of a cat on the wall.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's look from the cat to Kavitha suggest she was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she was interested and wanted to share the cat with Kavitha, since she pointed as well. It could also mean she was checking Kavitha's reaction.

qa.q: What might Kavitha say to Ayesha's mother?
qa.a: Kavitha might describe what they saw, that Ayesha follows a pointing finger and shares her attention, and if the mother has any questions about her child's development she can ask a paediatrician.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Kavitha's naming of the cat?
qa.a: She may feel that her attention is noticed and welcomed, and that a shared look comes with a word attached, which helps her learn.

grounding: A toddler follows a caregiver with her eyes and looks where the adult points, sharing attention on an object.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage: Evening on the farm. Sonali sat on the cot outside the house while her father, Pradeep, walked to the cowshed. Her eyes followed him the whole way. When he came back, he crouched beside her and pointed up. "Look, Sonali, parrot!" She turned her head and found the green bird in the mango tree. Then she looked back at his face, grinned, and stabbed her own little finger toward the branch.

qa.q: Where was the parrot?
qa.a: In the mango tree.

qa.q: What does Sonali's look back at Pradeep's face suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was interested in the parrot and wanted to share it with him, feeling safe and connected; it could also be that she was checking she had found the right thing.

qa.q: How could Pradeep keep building this shared looking?
qa.a: He could keep pointing at things around the farm, naming them, and waiting for her to point back.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Sonali points at the branch herself?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased and close to her, seeing that she followed his point and shared it back. 😊

grounding: A toddler follows her father with her eyes and looks where he points, sharing attention on a bird.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage:
At the bus stop in Toronto, Dalia pointed across the road. "Leila, look, the big red bus!" For weeks Leila had rarely looked where Dalia pointed, and Dalia had written it down to ask about at the check-up.
Today Leila turned, found the bus and kept her eyes on it as it pulled in. Then she looked up at Dalia and said, "Bus."
Dalia smiled, and still kept the note in her bag for the doctor.

qa.q: What did Dalia point to across the road?
qa.a: The big red bus.

qa.q: What might Dalia have been feeling when Leila looked at the bus and said "Bus"?
qa.a: Probably relieved and happy, after weeks of worry that Leila rarely followed her pointing; she still seems a little unsure, since she kept the note.

qa.q: Was keeping the note for the doctor a good idea, and why?
qa.a: Yes, because a paediatrician can look at the whole picture, and asking costs nothing even if today went well.

qa.q: How does Leila seem to experience the moment?
qa.a: She seems interested in the bus and pleased to share it, looking up at Dalia to name it.

grounding: A mother notices her toddler starting to follow her point and still plans to raise the earlier worry with the doctor.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage: I'm Imran, and on Sunday I took my little cousin Rafiq to watch the colony cricket match. Every time someone hit the ball, I pointed and shouted, "There it goes!" At first Rafiq just stared at my finger. By the third hit, his eyes flew off my hand and found the ball rolling toward the boundary. Then he looked straight back at me and laughed. I'm not sure he understood cricket. Maybe he just liked us looking together.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do by the third hit?
qa.a: His eyes flew off Imran's hand and found the ball rolling toward the boundary.

qa.q: What might Rafiq's laugh after looking back at Imran show?
qa.a: It likely shows delight at sharing the moment with Imran and trust in him, more than understanding the game; he may simply have enjoyed the ball moving.

qa.q: What small step could help Rafiq follow points more easily?
qa.a: Pointing at big, moving things and saying their name, as Imran did, then waiting for him to look back.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran when Rafiq looks back at him?
qa.a: Imran feels included and amused, though unsure what Rafiq understood, and values the looking together.

grounding: A cousin sees a toddler move from staring at a pointing finger to following it and sharing attention on the ball.

subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage:
A Sunday in March: Swati pointed at a red kite over the park. “Yash, look!” Yash stared at her finger, not the sky.
At his check-up she mentioned it. The doctor said to keep pointing things out and to come back if she stayed worried.
A Sunday in April: she pointed at a crow. Yash's eyes followed her arm all the way to the wall.
A Sunday in May: Yash pointed at a dog himself, then turned to check she was looking too.

qa.q: What did Yash stare at in March instead of the kite?
qa.a: Yash stared at her finger, not the sky.

qa.q: What does Yash turning to check Swati was looking suggest he felt in May?
qa.a: It suggests he was interested and wanted to share the dog with her, showing trust that she would look too.

qa.q: What did Swati do that was sensible?
qa.a: She kept pointing things out in play and mentioned her early worry to the doctor instead of ignoring it or panicking.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati when Yash points at the dog and checks on her?
qa.a: She is likely relieved and happy, because they are now sharing attention on the same thing.

grounding: It shows a toddler learning to follow a parent's point and share attention, with an early worry raised with the doctor.
